criterion_notes.c1: Examines the monthly household cost of basic municipal drinking water services (6,000 gallons/month, representing the basic household sanitary requirement for a family of four) across more than 2,000 US municipalities, directly addressing economic access/affordability of household drinking water service.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 READING. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2 ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this paper qualifies ('yes') because it tests municipal institutional, administrative, political, and regulatory variables as predictors of basic drinking water bills—specifically mayor vs. non-mayor municipal form of government, municipal government size (FTEs per capita), wholesale water purchasing, municipal fiscal conditions (revenue, debt ratio, utility spending), resident political ideology, and recent Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) health-based violations. Under the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope, however, it fails ('no'): utility ownership is held constant (all 2,119 systems are municipally owned and operated), state rate-setting and regulatory frameworks are unanalysed fixed effects rather than measured rules, tariff schedules are collapsed into the dependent price variable rather than tested as tariff or cost-recovery rules governing access, and the explanatory variables are general municipal political/organizational characteristics, financial balances, and water-quality/source conditions rather than rule-type mechanisms (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or ownership/regulatory structure directly governing household service access).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains original quantitative empirical analysis combining primary collection of municipal drinking water rate schedules (November 2021 to May 2022) for 2,161 municipalities with the Municipal Drinking Water Database (MDWD), US Census/ACS, EPA SDWIS, and VEST political ideology data, estimated on n = 2,119 municipalities using state (and EPA-region) fixed-effects OLS regressions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports monthly household cost in dollars for 6,000 gallons of basic drinking water services (incorporating fixed charges and volumetric rates), an outcome directly relevant to household drinking water affordability (mean $38.60, range $5.00 to $163.40, benchmarked at 3.3% of federal minimum-wage monthly income).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (contiguous US municipalities with population >= 10,000 that own and operate a drinking water utility; analytic n = 2,119), municipal-level fiscal, demographic/ideological, organizational, and environmental exposures, household basic water cost outcome, and cross-sectional fixed-effects OLS regression design.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper uses a new, national dataset to examine the social, political, environmental, and institutional drivers of the cost of basic drinking water services, measured as the cost to households of 6000 gal of water per month.
Water cost is a direct reflection of what it would cost a household to use 6000 gal of water in 1 month given relevant fixed charges and volumetric rates.
We use the publicly available MDWD (Hughes et al. 2022, 2023), which is comprised of the US municipalities with a population of 10,000 or more that own and operate a drinking water system.

Expected relationships between the cost of basic drinking water services and fiscal conditions, community characteristics, organizational structure, and environmental risk. All variables are measured at the municipal scale.
States represents state-level fixed effects, which account for the fact that state governments may impose unique conditions on public service provisioning and drinking water rate setting.
We estimate the following linear regression model using OLS in Stata version 16. Robust standard errors corrected for clustering by state are implemented for all models.
The cost of basic drinking water services (6000 gal per month) in the United States ranges from $5 to $163.40, with an average value of $38.60 (Figure 2).

raw_response.exposure: Municipal fiscal conditions (revenue per capita, debt ratio, water utility expenditures per capita), community characteristics (% Black, % Hispanic, logged population size, population density, median household income, conservative political ideology), municipal/utility organizational characteristics (municipal FTEs per capita, mayor form of government dummy, wholesale purchased water dummy), and environmental/compliance risk factors (recent SDWA health-based violation, aridity moisture index, surface vs. groundwater dependence)
raw_response.outcome: Monthly household cost of basic drinking water services (Water cost, in USD, for 6,000 gallons per month based on fixed charges and volumetric rates; also contextualized as share of minimum-wage gross monthly income)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Contiguous US municipalities with population >= 10,000 that own and operate a drinking water system (rate data collected for 2,161 municipalities; regression analytic sample n = 2,119 municipalities/utilities; unit of analysis: municipality/municipal drinking water system)
raw_response.rationale: This empirical cross-sectional study analyses the drivers of monthly household bills for basic drinking water services (6,000 gallons/month) across 2,119 municipally owned US water systems using state fixed-effects OLS regressions. Under the literal/plain wording of Criterion 2, the study would be included because it tests municipal institutional, administrative, political, and regulatory variables (mayor vs. non-mayor form of city government, municipal FTE size, wholesale water purchasing, fiscal debt/spending ratios, voter political ideology, and past SDWA health-based violations). However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, it is excluded (E03, Wrong exposure): utility ownership does not vary (only municipally owned systems are included), state regulatory frameworks governing water rates are absorbed as unanalysed state fixed effects, tariff structures are collapsed into the outcome variable rather than tested as tariff or cost-recovery rules governing service access, and the explanatory variables represent general municipal political/organizational features, financial balances, and water-source/compliance conditions rather than rule-type legal or administrative mechanisms directly governing household service access.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional quantitative observational study (state fixed-effects OLS regression)
